posts.caption: The vet's truck pulled in at 1:10 for what he called a quick look at the big mare's eye. He said it twice. Quick look. In and out. I've had her eleven years, so I texted my sister that I'd be late for dinner before he even got his bag open. She let him get the light out. She let him get close. Then she lifted that front foot, set it down very gently right next to his boot, and left it there. We negotiated for most of the afternoon. The eye was fine. His schedule was not.
posts.first: My old farrier used to book my draft cross last on Fridays, with nothing after her. He said it wasn't personal. He brought a folding chair, a thermos and a radio, and some weeks he used all three. In twenty years he never once raised his voice at her.

posts.caption: I buy carrots in the twenty-five pound sack from the feed store now, because the little grocery store bags were a waste of everyone's time. The sack lives in the feed room, on a pallet, behind a door that latches. Pudding found it on day two. I came in at 4:30 to do evening grain and he was standing with his entire face pressed into the burlap, perfectly still, like he'd been placed there. He hadn't eaten one. He was just near them. Supervising. I gave him two to make him leave. He took them and stayed.
posts.first: My mother kept sugar cubes in her apron pocket for forty years, and every horse she ever met knew it. They'd follow her down the fence line like ducklings. She swore she never gave them any. The bottom of every apron she owned was covered in nose prints.

posts.quote: Twelve years of trail rides past the same mailbox. Today he noticed it. We took the long way home. The mailbox won.
posts.first: My gelding refused to walk past a blue tarp on the neighbor's woodpile for three weeks straight. On the fourth week the neighbor folded it up and put it away. The next morning he stopped dead and snorted at the empty spot where it used to be.

posts.caption: Our farrier started coming out in 2007, when he was a skinny kid with a borrowed truck and the old gray was a fourteen year old show horse with opinions. Now the farrier has a bad knee and a grandson, and the gray is twenty-six with white whiskers. Every six weeks they do the same slow dance. Front left, front right, a rest, a long stretch, another rest. They both groan when they straighten up. Neither of them hurries. I've stopped offering to help, because it isn't my appointment.
posts.first: When my old mare turned thirty, the farrier started bringing her a peppermint at every appointment. He said he was just being polite. Last spring I saw a bag of them on his dashboard with her name written on it in marker. He's never mentioned it, so neither have I.

posts.caption: I braided her mane the night before the show, all twenty-two braids, by headlamp, in the trailer aisle. I washed her tail twice. I put on her clean sheet and went to bed at midnight feeling like a professional. At six the next morning I found her in the warm-up field. She had worked the sheet off overnight and hung it on the fence. The sheet was spotless. The braids were spotless. One entire side of her, from ear to hock, was the color of a creek bed. We were in the ring at 7:20. The judge said she had presence.
posts.first: The first time I took my mare to a show, I spent two hours on her white socks with chalk and an old toothbrush. The minute I turned my back she stepped into her water bucket. Not to drink. Just to stand in it, one sock at a time.

posts.caption: Three peppermints fell out of my good wool coat at my niece's wedding in June, right during the vows. They crinkle. Everyone heard. I've stopped pretending I can own a coat without them, because the second I walk into the barn in any jacket at all, the bay mare comes over and stands with her nose about an inch from the pocket. She doesn't nudge. She doesn't paw. She just waits, very politely, breathing on it. It works every single time. My husband says I've been trained. He isn't wrong.
posts.first: My grandmother wore the same brown canvas barn coat for thirty years. After she passed, my aunt hung it on the fence while she cleaned out the tack room, and the old gelding walked straight over and checked the pocket. There was still one peppermint in it.
